Consult Summary:
- Acute viral upper respiratory infection with dry cough and nasal symptoms in a patient with diabetes and hypertension; consideration of concurrent ACE inhibitor cough; plan emphasizes home monitoring and red-flag guidance with diabetes/HTN caution.

History:
- Presenting complaint: 5 days of cough (dry) and runny nose; nasal discharge described as green; no chest pain, no shortness of breath, no coughing up blood.
- Timeline: Symptoms began ~5 days ago; cough is frequent (approximately every 20–30 minutes); nasal symptoms present; no ongoing vomiting or diarrhea now; patient reports some feverish feeling (hot to touch, occasionally chilly) but no measured fever.
- Associated symptoms: No chest pain, no SOB, no hemoptysis; nasal congestion with continuous tearing; no rashes; muscle aches; no headaches or vision changes.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors: Lemon sips (home remedy) provide throat soothing and help sleep; fluids and regular intake maintained.
- Other systems: Appetite and fluid intake preserved; no vomiting; bowel movements initially had diarrhea around onset but currently normal.
- Pertinent negatives: No measured fever; no SOB or chest pain; no blood in nasal discharge; no significant weight change reported.
- PMH: Diabetes mellitus and hypertension.
- Medications: Metformin; lisinopril. Lisinopril dose not explicitly documented in the transcript; patient stated “two hundred” when asked for dose, but the documentation notes “dose/route/frequency not documented.” Metformin dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies: Hay fever (allergic rhinitis); no drug allergies reported.
- Social history: Office manager; lives with partner and dog; drinks alcohol socially (“the odd cherry”); smoking status not documented.
- Family history: Not discussed.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Working diagnosis: Acute viral upper respiratory infection with dry cough and rhinitis; possible concurrent ACE inhibitor–associated cough; no evidence of acute bacterial pneumonia or other urgent chest pathology based on history.
- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Acute viral upper respiratory infection with possible acute bronchitis
    - Supporting: 5-day course, dry cough, nasal symptoms, systemic warmth sensation; generally self-limiting.
    - Opposing: Green nasal discharge; no objective fever documented.
  - ACE inhibitor–induced cough
    - Supporting: Lisinopril use; dry, non-productive cough.
    - Opposing: Onset timing relative to lisinopril initiation not documented.
  - Acute sinusitis with postnasal drip contributing to cough
    - Supporting: Green nasal discharge; nasal symptoms.
    - Opposing: No facial pain/tocal tenderness or fever documented; short duration favors viral etiology.
- Issue 1: Acute viral upper respiratory infection with possible bronchitis
  - Plan:
    - Continue supportive care: lemon-based relief (monitor for excessive paracetamol exposure; avoid concurrent paracetamol-containing products with lemon sip remedy).
    - Hydration and rest; oral fluids maintained.
    - Cough management: daytime cough syrup not advised; nighttime use allowed if sleep disturbance persists.
    - Temperature monitoring: obtain a home thermometer; if fever persists >37.5–38°C or spikes repeatedly, or cough worsens, re-contact.
    - Antibiotics: not routinely indicated at this time; consider if symptoms fail to resolve or worsen or red-flag features emerge (e.g., increasing purulent sputum, chest pain, shortness of breath).
    - Diabetes/BP considerations: ensure regular GP checkups for diabetes and hypertension; maintain routine monitoring.
- Issue 2: Possible ACE inhibitor–related cough
  - Plan:
    - Review temporal relation to lisinopril; if cough persists or worsens and other etiologies are not confirmed, consider discussing with GP about alternative antihypertensive therapy.
- Issue 3: Possible sinusitis/postnasal drip
  - Plan:
    - Symptomatic management; monitor for facial pain, fever, or prolonged symptoms beyond 7–10 days.
- General plan:
  - Do not initiate antibiotics unless clinical course worsens or fails to improve.
  - Avoid multiple paracetamol-containing products with lemon-based relief.
  - Return to clinic or contact PCP if fever develops or symptoms worsen; monitor for red-flag symptoms (shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing up blood).
  - Ensure ongoing diabetes and blood pressure monitoring with primary care.
  - Check temperature at home and report persistent fever or prolonged symptoms.

Document Quality:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: No documented vitals or comprehensive physical exam; no explicit smoking status; exact lisinopril dose/frequency not documented.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified; DDx aligns with transcript.
- Transcript quality: Sufficient to support assessment and management given self-limited viral URI focus; some details (vital signs, full exam) not recorded.
